claim: Limb movements associated with anti-parasite defenses can enhance acoustic signal attraction in male little torrent frogs (Amolops torrentis).
source: Recently we showed that limb movements associated with anti-parasite defenses can enhance acoustic signal attraction in male little torrent frogs (Amolops torrentis), which suggests a potential pathway for physical movements to become co-opted into mating displays (Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Zhao et al., 2022) and is the main finding being defended in this response.

claim: Physical movements have been viewed as the raw material of visual signals for many years.
source: Physical movements have been viewed as the raw material of visual signals for many years (Harper, 1991; Johnsgard, 1962).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Harper (1991) and Johnsgard (1962).

claim: Little is known about how physical displays evolve and become a part of communicative systems.
source: However, little is known about how physical displays evolve and become a part of communicative systems.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: According to the sensory exploitation hypothesis, physical movements may be incorporated into multimodal systems if they enhance the attractiveness of male individuals.
source: According to the sensory exploitation hypothesis, physical movements may be incorporated into multimodal systems if they enhance the attractiveness of male individuals (Ryan, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ryan (1998) and describes a theoretical framework.

claim: Movements associated with anti-parasite behavior can act on female perception and may thereby affect the evolution of a multimodal display in little torrent frogs (Amolops torrentis).
source: Recently we showed that movements associated with anti-parasite behavior can act on female perception and may thereby affect the evolution of a multimodal display in little torrent frogs (Amolops torrentis) (Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior work (Zhao et al., 2022).

claim: Hind foot lifting (HFL) and arm waving (AW) are the two movements most strongly preferred in playback experiments by female little torrent frogs.
source: Anderson et al. suggest that the two movements most strongly preferred in playback experiments by females – hind foot lifting (HFL) and arm waving (AW) – are not associated with the presence of eavesdropping parasites
evidence: This claim is stated as a finding from playback experiments, though presented in the context of Anderson et al.'s interpretation.

claim: Anderson et al.'s reanalysis included observations from non-calling males which had been recorded outside of a breeding context.
source: Most importantly, they included observations from non-calling males (which had been recorded outside of a breeding context for our control videos), whereas we analysed data from actively displaying males only.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used in Anderson et al.'s reanalysis.

claim: Many silent males were observed to be undisturbed by parasites and produced few limb movements.
source: Many silent males were observed to be undisturbed by parasites and produced few limb movements (Supplementary file 1 in Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to supplementary data from the authors' prior work.

claim: The inclusion of data from silent males greatly underestimates any effect of parasites on limb movements.
source: Thus, the inclusion of data from silent males greatly underestimates any effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that silent males produce few movements and are undisturbed by parasites.

claim: All movements were produced around parasites in calling individuals.
source: Similar to previous results, our new analysis found that all movements were produced around parasites in calling individuals (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the new GLMM analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: The proportion of parasite-induced movements is likely to be underestimated in the original study.
source: Second, the proportion of parasite-induced movements is likely to be underestimated in our original study.
evidence: This is an inference based on the methodology used in the original study.

claim: For parasite-induced displays, only movements that occurred when parasites landed on the body of frogs or moved very close to them were included.
source: For parasite-induced displays, we only included movements that occurred when parasites landed on the body of frogs or moved very close to them.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the original study.

claim: When taking additional environmental variables into account, all four movements tested on female preferences increased with parasite presence.
source: When taking additional environmental variables into account, we now find that all four movements tested on female preferences increased with parasite presence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the new GLMM analysis presented in Table 1, which includes noise level as a covariate.

claim: It is not clear how effective the limb movements, in particular a movement such as hind-foot lifting, are as an anti-predator strategy.
source: It is important to note, however, that it is not clear how effective the limb movements, in particular a movement such as hind-foot lifting, are as an anti-predator strategy.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty about the functional effectiveness of certain movements.

claim: Different limb movements may be produced simultaneously when they are controlled by the same neuronal and/or physiological pathway.
source: Mechanistically, different limb movements may be produced (somewhat) simultaneously (for example, when they are controlled by the same neuronal and/or physiological pathway).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for why different movements might co-occur.

claim: Some movements may have evolved after females started to pay attention, and thus immediately functioned in mate attraction.
source: Theoretically, some movements may have evolved after females started to pay attention, and thus immediately functioned in mate attraction.
evidence: This is a theoretical speculation about the evolutionary sequence of movement functions.

claim: If movements recruited the same mechanism as anti-parasite movements, then we would expect to find a relation with parasite pressure, even if the movement lost or never possessed an anti-parasite function.
source: If such movements recruited (part of) the same mechanism, then we would also expect to find a relation with parasite pressure, even if the movement lost or never possessed an anti-parasite function.
evidence: This is a logical inference about expected patterns based on shared mechanisms.

claim: The role of limb displays in male–male competition can be easily observed and recorded in the wild.
source: The role of limb displays in male–male competition can be easily observed and recorded in the wild, whereas observing or manipulating male–female interactions is challenging in many species.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical feasibility of different types of observations.

claim: Observing or manipulating male–female interactions is challenging in many species.
source: The role of limb displays in male–male competition can be easily observed and recorded in the wild, whereas observing or manipulating male–female interactions is challenging in many species.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical challenges of studying certain behaviors.

claim: Data on female choice behavior is rare in studies on limb displays in torrent frogs.
source: Anderson et al. summarize studies on limb displays in torrent frogs and show that data on female choice behavior is rare
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, attributed to Anderson et al.

claim: The rarity of female choice data does not mean that female choice behavior has a smaller role than male–male competition.
source: Anderson et al. summarize studies on limb displays in torrent frogs and show that data on female choice behavior is rare, but we disagree with the statement that this means that female choice behavior has a smaller role than male–male competition.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of the literature gap.

claim: When studies address multimodal displays in the context of intra- and intersexual interactions simultaneously, they typically show that males and females pay attention to similar cues.
source: Only very few studies have addressed multimodal displays in the context of intra- and intersexual interactions simultaneously, but when they do, they typically show that males and females pay attention to similar cues (Halfwerk et al., 2014; James et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Halfwerk et al. (2014) and James et al. (2022).

claim: In animal communication, it is generally assumed that male responses to playback reflect female responses and thus can be used to study signal evolution in a broad comparative framework.
source: In animal communication, it is generally assumed (although perhaps wrongly) that male responses to playback reflect female responses and thus can be used to study signal evolution in a broad comparative framework.
evidence: This is a statement about a general assumption in the field of animal communication.

claim: The assumption that male responses to playback reflect female responses may be wrong.
source: In animal communication, it is generally assumed (although perhaps wrongly) that male responses to playback reflect female responses and thus can be used to study signal evolution in a broad comparative framework.
evidence: This is a speculative caveat about a common assumption in the field.

claim: The data on males is observational and does not provide evidence for causal relationships.
source: Our data on males is observational and does not provide evidence for causal relationships, a point on which we agree with Anderson et al.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the observational data.

claim: The novelty of the paper lies in proposing a novel hypothesis of how and why multimodal displays evolve, namely via a process of co-option and possibly sensory exploitation.
source: The novelty of our paper lies in the fact that we propose a novel hypothesis of how and why multimodal displays evolve, namely via a process of co-option and possibly sensory exploitation.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical contribution of the authors' work.

claim: Studying the evolutionary history of multimodal displays requires a phylogenetic comparative approach.
source: Studying the evolutionary history of multimodal displays, such as the limb movements produced during calling in torrent frogs, requires a phylogenetic comparative approach.
evidence: This is a statement about the appropriate methodology for studying evolutionary history.

claim: For phylogenetic comparative studies, data on male–male interactions might be more useful than data on male–female interactions, given the challenges of collecting such data in the field.
source: For such a study, data on male–male interactions might be more useful than data on male–female interactions, given the challenges of collecting such data in the field.
evidence: This is an inference about practical considerations for future research.

claim: Several limb movements enhance the attractiveness of a calling male.
source: Finally, our data on female choice is highly novel because we show that several limb movements enhance the attractiveness of a calling male, which is a prerequisite for the co-option of cues into multimodal displays.
evidence: This claim is presented as a finding from the authors' female choice experiments.

claim: Enhanced attractiveness of calling males due to limb movements is a prerequisite for the co-option of cues into multimodal displays.
source: Finally, our data on female choice is highly novel because we show that several limb movements enhance the attractiveness of a calling male, which is a prerequisite for the co-option of cues into multimodal displays.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about the evolutionary process of co-option.

claim: Anderson et al. included silent males outside of a breeding context in their reanalysis.
source: However, they included silent males outside of a breeding context in their reanalysis, and may therefore underestimate the effect size.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used in Anderson et al.'s reanalysis.

claim: Only calling males are relevant for studying breeding behaviors.
source: This study focused on breeding behaviors in which only calling males are relevant.
evidence: This is a methodological justification based on the focus of the study.

claim: Parasite presence was mediated by calling behaviors because parasites often used acoustic signals to find frogs.
source: Moreover, parasite presence was mediated by calling behaviors because parasites often used acoustic signals to find frogs.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism by which parasites locate frogs.

claim: Individuals with the same proportion of a specific movement may have different impact if the absolute total number of limb movements is different.
source: Anderson et al. proposed that individuals with the same proportion of a specific movement may have different impact if the absolute total number of limb movements is different.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration raised by Anderson et al. and acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Overall movements were treated as random factor to avoid potential statistical bias.
source: So the overall movements were treated as random factor to avoid potential statistical bias.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methodology used in the new analysis.

claim: The noise intensity of the habitat may vary in different locations and could affect the production of limb movements.
source: The noise intensity of the habitat may vary in different locations and could affect the production of limb movements, as pointed out by Anderson et al.
evidence: This is a potential confounding factor acknowledged by the authors and attributed to Anderson et al.

claim: A likelihood ratio test did not show a significant reduction in explanatory power when comparing a full model with a collapsed model that excluded a random factor of male ID (χ2=0, df=1, P=1).
source: A likelihood ratio test (χ2=0, df = 1, P=1) did not show a significant reduction in explanatory power when we compared a full model (which included all terms of interest) with a collapsed model (which excluded a random factor of male ID).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical test results reported in the text.

claim: Only overall movement was treated as the random factor in the GLMM to avoid singularities.
source: Only overall movement was treated as the random factor in order to avoid singularities (Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methodology used in the analysis.

claim: Individual and environmental variation may affect parasite distribution and limb display.
source: Individual and environmental variation may affect parasite distribution and limb display.
evidence: This is a statement about potential confounding factors in the study.

claim: The GLMM evaluated the relationship between the frequency of parasite visit and the number of limb movements, while controlling for individual and environmental variation.
source: The GLMM evaluated the relationship between the frequency of parasite visit and the number of limb movements, while controlling for individual and environmental variation, and was therefore appropriate to test whether the presence of parasites increased limb movement.
evidence: This is a description of what the statistical analysis accomplished.
